content: The expertise of the members spans various thematic areas within maternal and perinatal health. From the Maternal and Perinatal Health Guideline Development Group (MPH-GDG) pool, 17 external experts and relevant stakeholders were invited to form the Guideline Development Group (GDG) tasked with updating this recommendation. The selected individuals represented a diverse group with expertise in research, guideline development methodologies, and clinical policies and programs related to maternal and perinatal health. The GDG evaluated and interpreted the evidence presented by guideline methodologists to formulate the recommendations. After the GDG meeting, the group reviewed and approved the final guideline document. The members of this group are listed in Annex 1. An External Review Group, consisting of eight technical experts with a focus on evidence-informed obstetric care, was also involved. None of its members declared any conflicts of interest. These experts reviewed the final document to identify factual errors and provided feedback on the clarity of language, contextual issues, and implications for the implementation of the WHO recommendations on drug treatment for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy. However, they did not alter the recommendations formulated by the GDG. The names and affiliations of the external reviewers are acknowledged in the document but do not imply their endorsement of the recommendations. A systematic review addressing the key question was commissioned with the support of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group. The WHO Steering Group reviewed and contributed to the protocol and collaborated closely with the Cochrane Group to appraise the evidence using the GRADE methodology. Representatives from the Cochrane Group attended the GDG meeting to present an overview of the evidence, GRADE tables, and respond to technical queries. Representatives from external organizations, including USAID, the Maternal and Child Survival Program (MCSP)/Jhpiego, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM), the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), and the Population Council, participated as observers in the GDG meeting. These organizations, with a history of collaboration with WHO in guideline dissemination and implementation, are among the implementers of the recommendations. The list of observers is provided in Annex 1. The critical and important outcomes for this guideline were aligned with those prioritized in the WHO recommendations on the prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. These outcomes were identified through a search of key sources of systematic reviews and prioritization by the 2011 GDG panel. All outcomes were included in the scope of this document for evidence searching, retrieval, grading, and recommendation formulation. The list of outcomes is provided in Annex 2. Evidence on the effects of antihypertensive drugs for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy was derived from an updated systematic review conducted in 2018 with the support of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group. This review served as the primary source of evidence on the benefits and harms of antihypertensive drugs for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy. The review followed Cochrane's standard procedures and included randomized controlled trials evaluating antihypertensive medications compared to placebo, no treatment, or other antihypertensive drugs. Relevant data were entered into Review Manager 5 (RevMan) software, customized for key comparisons and outcomes, and exported to GRADE profiler software (GRADEpro) for critical appraisal. Evidence profiles, including GRADE summary of findings tables, were prepared for comparisons of interest. For questions related to values, equity, acceptability, and feasibility, findings were derived from two recent qualitative systematic reviews commissioned by WHO. These reviews explored women's experiences with antenatal care services and the provision and uptake of routine antenatal care. The systematic review team used the GRADE-CERQual tool to assess the quality of qualitative evidence, assigning confidence levels (high, moderate, low, very low) based on methodological limitations, adequacy of data, coherence, and relevance. The WHO Steering Group supervised the preparation of summary findings tables and narrative evidence summaries using the GRADE evidence-to-decision (EtD) framework. This framework systematically considered evidence on prioritized interventions across domains such as effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. Judgments on the impact of interventions on each domain informed the decision-making process. The GDG reviewed the EtD frameworks, draft recommendations, and preliminary feedback during an online meeting on July 31, 2019. The purpose of the meeting was to reach a consensus on each recommendation, including its direction and specific context, based on the evidence presented and the GDG members' judgments. The GDG categorized recommendations as follows: (1) Recommended, (2) Not recommended, (3) Recommended only in specific contexts (context-specific recommendation), or (4) Recommended only in the context of rigorous research (research-context recommendation). The GDG reviewed and discussed the evidence summary during the meeting, applying additional criteria based on the GRADE EtD framework to determine the direction and strength of the recommendations. Decisions were made by consensus, defined as agreement by at least three-quarters of participants, with no opposition expressed by GDG members. Following the meeting, the WHO Steering Group prepared a draft recommendation document reflecting the deliberations and decisions of the participants. This draft was sent electronically to GDG members and the External Review Group for final review and approval. After peer review, the WHO Steering Group made modifications to correct factual errors and improve clarity. The recommendations adopted by the GDG include offering antihypertensive drug treatment to women with non-severe hypertension during pregnancy in the context of good-quality antenatal care follow-up. Oral alpha-agonists (e.g., methyldopa) and beta-blockers are considered effective treatment options for non-severe hypertension during pregnancy. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine the superiority of one drug over another. Methyldopa and beta-blockers likely reduce the risk of severe hypertension, though beta-blockers may slightly increase the risk of side effects. Calcium channel blockers may increase the risk of developing proteinuria or pre-eclampsia.
